changes.before: Both length-only and Logistic-L1 use a training-fitted StandardScaler followed by LogisticRegression. changes.after: The labeled comparison quantifies the detection trade-off of scheme neutralization. At the two frozen operating points in Table 4.16, the refitted candidate produces 251 fewer false positives and 184 fewer true positives. These paired counts distinguish beneficial false-alert reductions from suppressed detections, giving the invariance result its operational meaning.

changes.before: D achieves exact scheme invariance on the tested pairs, but the proposed joint detection improvement is rejected. Normalization, refitting and recalibration reduce false positives while also losing detections, and FPR remains above the required ceiling. Implementing the intended transformation therefore succeeds without producing the class separation needed for a useful detector redesign.
changes.after: D establishes exact scheme invariance and measures the accompanying detection trade-off. Normalization, refitting and recalibration reduce both false positives and true-positive detections, with FPR remaining above the required ceiling. The engineering finding is that representation stability and class separation are distinct properties, each requiring labeled evaluation when the detector is redesigned. The joint requirement evaluates both properties together.

changes.before: A prefix change has a substantial effect even with the structural model held fixed (Table 4.21). HTTP detects all 69 gold positives but flags every certified negative. With Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS), certified false positives fall from 2,261 to 50, while gold detections fall from 69 to 22. The change removes 2,211 false positives at the cost of 47 true-positive detections. FPR remains 2.0024%, above 1%, and recall declines to 31.8841%. Thus, prefix replacement alone cannot meet the detection requirement.
changes.after: A prefix change has a substantial effect even with the structural model held fixed (Table 4.21). HTTP detects all 69 gold positives but flags every certified negative. The change removes 2,211 false positives at the cost of 47 true-positive detections. FPR remains 2.0024%, above 1%, and recall declines to 31.8841%. The intervention quantifies the detection cost of prefix replacement and establishes the need to evaluate normalization against both classes.

changes.before: Paired errors explain the routing constraint: common false positives survive selection between unchanged decisions. Representation tests identify a separate target. changes.before: CyberSentinel connects URL representation, monitoring and selective execution to measured outcomes. Structural features add 64.07 percentage points of internal recall within the benchmark. Validation controls identify format–class association, and a fixed-weight intervention establishes external scheme sensitivity. A separate refit achieves exact invariance across 8,622 pairs with measured detection losses. Together, these experiments provide concrete tests of representation stability and its consequences for labeled detection.
changes.after: CyberSentinel connects URL representation, monitoring and selective execution to measured outcomes. Structural features add 64.07 percentage points of internal recall within the benchmark. judgment: Strengthened interpretation and removed repetitive negative verdicts. The measured results, formal acceptance decisions, deployment status and substantive limitations remain explicit.
